paragraphs: Autoregressive image generators predict sequences of visual tokens drawn from a large vocabulary. Usually, that vocabulary is treated as an unstructured collection, even though nearby token embeddings can represent similar visual meanings. The paper argues that ignoring these relationships makes prediction unnecessarily difficult and limits both training efficiency and image quality.

The proposed method, Manifold-Aligned Semantic Clustering, or MASC, organizes the token vocabulary into a semantic tree. It builds this hierarchy directly from the codebook’s geometry, using a distance measure sensitive to that geometry and a clustering procedure guided by density. Prediction then becomes a structured task that can exploit relationships among tokens, giving the model useful organization before it learns to generate images.

The authors report training acceleration of up to 71% and an improvement in LlamaGen-XL’s FID from 2.87 to 2.49. They also find that MASC enables convergence in complex architectures. These results support treating vocabulary organization as a meaningful design choice alongside changes to the generator itself.
icml-2026-a-flat-vocabulary-or-a-rich-hi.tldr: MASC organizes visual tokens into a geometry-based hierarchy, improving autoregressive image generation quality and training efficiency.

paragraphs: Graph foundation models aim to learn reusable patterns from many graphs. Much of this work considers graphs with only one kind of feature, while real graphs can combine connections with text, images, and other information. The challenge is to represent these sources together so that their meanings align and their complementary information remains useful.

CAME addresses this challenge by first producing a graph representation for each modality separately. A collection of expert components then combines these representations, with routing decisions made at the level of individual representation dimensions. This gives the fusion mechanism finer control over how it combines information than treating each modality as a single indivisible contribution.

Training uses a cross-modal contrastive objective to encourage alignment across modalities while learning how to fuse them. Experiments across multiple tasks and diverse multimodal graph datasets demonstrate the framework’s effectiveness. The contribution is a coordinated approach to representing graph structure and heterogeneous features, making multimodal information part of the foundation model’s learning process.
icml-2026-a-graph-foundation-model-with-.tldr: CAME combines modality-specific graph representations through expert routing and contrastive alignment to learn from multimodal graphs.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards trains language models using responses whose success can be checked. Common algorithms effectively emphasize prompts on which the model sometimes succeeds, while giving less weight to very easy or very difficult prompts. This paper investigates whether training can improve by deliberately shifting more weight toward prompts with low observed success.

The authors examine asymmetric weighting schemes that can emphasize even prompts with no successful responses in the sampled group. Their findings distinguish two training settings: this approach particularly helps reinforcement learning started without prior supervised fine-tuning, where accuracy changes substantially during training. It helps less when supervised fine-tuning has already produced a model with high starting accuracy.

The theoretical analysis characterizes weights that minimize the time required to move from an initial success probability to a target under a fixed update budget. When success is rare and generating responses dominates cost, the optimal weights become asymmetric. The result supports emphasizing difficult prompts under these conditions, rather than prescribing one weighting rule for every training stage.
icml-2026-asymmetric-prompt-weighting-fo.tldr: Giving more weight to low-success prompts can accelerate verifiable-reward training, especially when reinforcement learning starts from low accuracy.

paragraphs: Remembering information and using it effectively are different capabilities. Existing agent evaluations often test recall of previous conversations or assess actions within a single session. Neither setting fully captures an agent that learns from acting, stores useful experience, and then relies on that experience to make decisions in later sessions.

MemoryArena evaluates this combined process through human-crafted tasks with deliberately interdependent subtasks. An agent must turn earlier actions and environmental feedback into memory, then use that memory to guide later actions toward the overall goal. The benchmark covers web navigation, planning under preferences, progressive information search, and sequential formal reasoning, placing memory inside an ongoing interaction loop.

The authors find that agents performing near the ceiling on existing long-context memory benchmarks such as LoCoMo can perform poorly in MemoryArena. This shows that strong recall scores do not by themselves establish effective memory use in the evaluated agentic setting. The benchmark makes the connection between stored experience and subsequent decisions an explicit target of evaluation.
icml-2026-benchmarking-agent-memory-in-i.tldr: MemoryArena tests whether agents can turn experience from earlier sessions into useful decisions on later, dependent tasks.

paragraphs: A unified image restoration model must handle different kinds of damage, including corruption that varies across an image. Many Transformer models still divide images into fixed patches before considering the damage type. This leaves the initial representation and final reconstruction unable to adapt their spatial handling directly to local degradation.

Flexible Image Transformer, or FIT, makes degradation information influence the full processing pipeline. A lightweight encoder estimates both an overall degradation vector and a spatial map. These signals control adaptive deformation during patch embedding and reconstruction, allowing the sampling arrangement to respond to damage. During training, task-token dropout also regularizes the model’s use of task information.

Across five standard benchmarks, FIT reports average PSNR values of 30.72 dB in the five-degradation setting and 32.83 dB in the three-degradation setting. The stated gains over recent unified methods range from 0.5 to 1.1 dB. Its learned spatial offsets also make the adaptation visible, connecting the model’s restoration behavior to where it changes its sampling.
icml-2026-bend-the-basics-degradation-aw.tldr: FIT adapts patch sampling and reconstruction to local image damage, improving unified restoration across multiple degradation settings.

paragraphs: Removing subtitles from video requires reconstructing the content they cover. Existing mask-guided diffusion approaches can require extensive annotations, full-model tuning, and explicit subtitle masks during use. CLEAR addresses these costs with a lightweight adaptation framework that learns guidance during training and removes subtitles without externally supplied masks at inference.

Its first stage uses pixel differences between video pairs as weak supervision for learning where content is occluded. This removes the need for dedicated annotations while learning subtitle features across languages. A second stage uses LoRA adapters for parameter-efficient refinement, preserving pretrained visual knowledge and supporting end-to-end removal without a separate detection module.

CLEAR also adjusts the influence of its learned guidance according to local quality estimates. This makes the guidance adaptive when subtitle styles vary or the guidance itself is noisy. The authors report superior multilingual subtitle removal while training only 0.77% of parameters. The approach therefore combines reduced training burden with a simpler inference process that no longer depends on mask sequences.
icml-2026-clear-context-aware-learning-w.tldr: CLEAR learns adaptive subtitle-removal guidance with lightweight adapters, enabling multilingual video editing without inference-time masks.

paragraphs: Teaching a group requires tracking individual understanding while keeping everyone moving toward a shared learning goal. The paper studies this challenge in clinical Socratic education, including settings resembling ward rounds. Models designed for one-on-one instruction can lose relevant context or pursue mismatched goals when several trainees need different kinds of guidance.

The authors introduce ClinEdu, a multi-agent simulator of these teaching interactions, and use it to construct ClinTeach, a large dataset of Socratic dialogues. Their teaching agent, ClinTutor-R1, uses an explicit internal thinking mechanism to represent both individual belief states and group consensus. This design makes the relationship between personal support and collective progress part of the agent’s reasoning.

Evaluation combines standard static benchmarks with interactive testing inside ClinEdu. The authors report improvements exceeding 20% over base models, performance comparable to proprietary reasoning models, and maintained instructional quality as student groups expand. These findings support the framework’s ability to coordinate group instruction in the evaluated settings, with interactive simulation serving as a central part of the evidence.
icml-2026-clintutor-r1-advancing-scalabl.tldr: ClinTutor-R1 models individual understanding and group consensus to improve clinical Socratic teaching across multiple trainees.

paragraphs: Robot policies often generate actions in chunks, but individually plausible chunks do not necessarily join into a smooth trajectory. FocalPolicy targets these transitions while balancing precision in the immediate future with planning farther ahead. The paper identifies discontinuities between chunks as a significant obstacle to learning coherent long-horizon manipulation.

Its training objective treats near-term and longer-term behavior differently. It supervises the timing and alignment of nearby actions directly, while regularizing frequency structure across several future chunks. This gives training a way to account for broader patterns of motion spanning chunk boundaries, rather than evaluating only the action distribution inside each separate chunk.

The policy also introduces locally anchored sampling during consistency flow-matching training to improve how efficiently target signals propagate. Experiments report stronger performance than existing approaches and show that the proposed modules also benefit other baselines. Together, the results support addressing cross-chunk coherence explicitly and pairing that objective with a training mechanism for learning complex action distributions efficiently.
icml-2026-focalpolicy-frequency-optimize.tldr: FocalPolicy combines near-term action alignment, longer-range frequency regularization, and locally anchored flow matching to improve motion coherence.

paragraphs: Visual dubbing changes a speaker’s lip movements to match new speech. Ideal training pairs would differ only in lip motion, but such data are scarce. Existing approaches often mask part of the video and fill it back in, which removes useful context and can cause identity changes, poor handling of occlusions, and degraded synchronization.

X-Dub uses a two-stage process to overcome the data problem. First, a mask-based inpainting model generates synthetic video pairs. Those pairs then train a separate mask-free editing model that becomes the final dubber. Keeping the complete video available to this final model preserves the context that masking would otherwise remove.

The framework also assigns different learning priorities across diffusion timesteps to separate potentially conflicting demands involving structure, lip movement, and texture. The authors introduce X-DubBench for evaluating diverse scenarios and report state-of-the-art synchronization, visual quality, and robustness. The central contribution is using generative inpainting to create training data for a different, context-preserving form of editing.
icml-2026-from-inpainting-to-editing-unl.tldr: X-Dub uses an inpainting model to generate training pairs for a mask-free visual dubber with improved synchronization and robustness.

paragraphs: A training dataset and objective can support many models with nearly equally good performance. This collection is called a Rashomon set. Examining it can reveal diversity among acceptable models and let users choose according to domain knowledge or preferences that are difficult to express directly in the training objective.

Computing these collections is expensive even for sparse decision trees, an interpretable model class. PRAXIS is an algorithm designed to approximate the decision-tree Rashomon set while sharply reducing memory use and runtime. Its purpose is to make exploring multiple valid models computationally practical, so that model choice can consider more than the score of a single fitted tree.

The authors report orders-of-magnitude resource improvements and find that PRAXIS regularly recovers almost all of the full set in their validation. That is an empirical recovery result for an approximation method. It supports broader use of Rashomon-set analysis on real-world datasets, where the cost of constructing the collection has otherwise constrained its usefulness.
icml-2026-from-rashomon-theory-to-praxis.tldr: PRAXIS efficiently approximates collections of near-optimal decision trees, regularly recovering almost all of the full set in validation.

paragraphs: Tendon-driven hands can have many muscles or cables acting on each joint. This creates a large action space with substantial redundancy, making direct policy search difficult. The paper uses that redundancy as a reason to search for a smaller action representation that still provides effective control over the hand’s mechanical motion.

Joint-Space Empowerment, or JoSE, measures how much control an agent has over its mechanical degrees of freedom. The authors formulate the search for a compact action space as an optimal precoding problem: a state-dependent mapping translates low-dimensional latent commands into high-dimensional actuator actions. They derive a closed-form solution under learned control-affine Gaussian dynamics, making that modeling assumption central to the analytical result.

Experiments with a musculoskeletal hand model and a tendon-driven robotic hand show improved dexterity, sample efficiency, and generalization for policies trained using the resulting action manifold. These findings support organizing redundant actuator commands around controllable mechanical features, and suggest optimal precoding as a broader framework for coordinating many actuators.
icml-2026-joint-space-empowerment-for-de.tldr: JoSE learns compact action spaces that coordinate redundant hand actuators, improving dexterity and learning efficiency in the evaluated systems.

paragraphs: Learning a distribution over permutations means learning which orderings are likely among a number of possibilities that grows factorially with sequence length. Existing diffusion approaches corrupt orderings through shuffle operations and learn to reverse those changes. The paper argues that these trajectories can become abrupt and increasingly difficult to reverse as sequences grow.

Soft-Rank Diffusion replaces shuffle-based corruption with a process built around soft ranks. It represents discrete positions through a continuous latent description of order, producing smoother trajectories while retaining a permutation-learning objective. For reconstruction, it introduces contextualized generalized Plackett–Luce denoisers, extending earlier parameterizations to better express dependencies in sequential decisions.

Experiments on sorting and combinatorial optimization show consistent improvements over prior diffusion baselines. The gains are especially strong for long sequences and tasks with an intrinsically sequential structure. The findings support changing both sides of the diffusion process: how an ordering is gradually corrupted and how the model represents the decisions needed to recover it.
icml-2026-learning-permutation-distribut.tldr: Soft-Rank Diffusion learns permutation distributions using smoother rank-based corruption and more expressive sequential denoisers.

paragraphs: Computational optics often needs to recover several physical properties from complex measurements. MMPD-Bench studies this problem for Mueller matrix observations, framing the recovery of multiple polarimetric modalities as modality fission. The learning task separates one rich observation into several physically meaningful outputs, connecting polarimetric decomposition with multimodal representation learning.

The benchmark provides data, standardized solutions, and evaluation procedures for deep surrogate models that replace iterative numerical inversion. It compares state-space models, vision transformers, conditional diffusion models, and neural operators. Evaluation considers perceptual fidelity, physical consistency, robustness, and computational efficiency together, so that producing visually convincing outputs is only one part of the assessment.

The analysis finds substantial trade-offs between accuracy and robustness in accelerated decomposition, exposing limitations of existing surrogates. The released resources include the full codebase and 21,412 high-resolution Mueller matrix observations collected through polarimetric measurements. This contribution creates a shared basis for studying how quickly learned models can recover multiple physical quantities while retaining reliable behavior.
icml-2026-mmpd-bench-bridging-multimodal.tldr: MMPD-Bench evaluates neural surrogates for polarimetric decomposition, revealing accuracy–robustness trade-offs across multiple model families.

paragraphs: Adapting vision-language-action models to new manipulation tasks often requires many demonstrations. DynVLA focuses on how actions evolve across an entire trajectory, seeking transferable motion structure beyond individual action imitation. The goal is to use prior motion knowledge to learn new tasks from a small number of examples.

Its Motion Dynamics Mechanism uses flow-matching inversion to extract compact latent representations from trajectories. Dynamics-Constrained Modeling then projects these representations onto a Dynamics Bank pretrained from diverse demonstrations. This bank grounds action generation in previously learned motion patterns, allowing the system to interpolate among existing action paradigms when representing new dynamics.

On 13 real-world tasks with around 20 demonstrations, the authors report a 15.8% improvement in average success rate over existing state-of-the-art systems. The result supports trajectory-level motion modeling as a useful basis for few-shot adaptation in the tested settings. The distinctive design choice is to make reusable dynamics an explicit intermediate representation connecting new examples to action generation.
icml-2026-motion-dynamics-learning-for-f.tldr: DynVLA adapts robots from few demonstrations by representing trajectory dynamics and connecting them to a bank of learned motion knowledge.

paragraphs: Neural networks transform the geometry of data as they learn useful representations. Because the underlying data manifold is usually unobserved, this paper approximates its local similarity structure with geometric graphs. Tracking these graphs provides a way to study how relationships among examples change during training.

The authors develop theoretical results about graph evolution in feedforward networks, identifying nonlinear activations as important drivers of feature geometry. They find that the observed transformations resemble discrete Ricci flow, a geometric process on graphs. This is presented as an analogy supported by theory and experiments, rather than an unrestricted identity between neural training and Ricci flow.

Experiments cover more than 20,000 feedforward networks trained on binary classification using synthetic and real-world datasets. As classes become separable, their graph representations develop community structure. Building on this connection, the authors introduce a framework for locally comparing learned transformations with discrete Ricci flow dynamics. Further experiments suggest relationships between geometric evolution, training time, and network depth.
icml-2026-neural-feature-geometry-evolve.tldr: Graph-based analysis suggests that feature geometry in trained feedforward networks evolves in ways resembling discrete Ricci flow.

paragraphs: A language model can understand a long input yet struggle to produce consistently long outputs. This paper examines variation across repeated generations, particularly changes in output length. Such instability matters because it affects both computational cost and the reliability of applications that depend on substantial generated text.

The authors introduce VOLTBench, a benchmark spanning heterogeneous tasks to measure length volatility systematically. They then analyze attention traces to identify common internal patterns associated with the instability. Their mitigation method, Structural Enforcement via Logits Boosting, or SELB, modifies decoding to encourage structural behavior that improves length accuracy and consistency without additional training.

Experiments on VOLTBench document severe instability in the evaluated mainstream models. For the reported base-model comparison, SELB increases mean output length by 148% and reduces length volatility by 69% while maintaining high generation quality. The study makes consistency across runs an explicit evaluation target and shows that a lightweight decoding intervention can improve that consistency in the tested setting.
icml-2026-on-stable-long-form-generation.tldr: VOLTBench measures unstable long-form output lengths, and SELB reduces that volatility through a training-free decoding intervention.

paragraphs: Transformer layers have different internal structures, yet training commonly applies the same learning rate to all of them. Layerwise Learning Rate, or LLR, uses properties of each layer’s weights to choose separate update rates. The aim is to balance progress across layers and improve training speed and generalization.

The method draws on Heavy-Tailed Self-Regularization theory, examining the spectral distribution of weight correlation matrices. Layers with weaker heavy-tailedness receive larger learning rates, while those with stronger heavy-tailedness receive smaller ones. This turns a measured property of the weights into a rule for distributing learning effort across the network.

Experiments span LLaMa through GPT-nano architectures, AdamW and Muon optimizers, and models from 60 million to 3 billion parameters. Reported speedups reach 1.5 times, while average zero-shot accuracy rises from 47.09% to 49.02% for 1B models and from 48.58% to 50.61% for 3B models. LLR also transfers nearly optimal settings from the uniform-rate baseline, reducing the tuning burden of adopting layer-specific rates.
icml-2026-one-lr-doesnt-fit-all-heavy-ta.tldr: LLR assigns layer-specific learning rates from weight spectral properties, improving training speed and zero-shot accuracy with low tuning overhead.

paragraphs: A network simulator can predict average delay accurately while missing rare long delays and fluctuations in timing. The paper identifies this weakness in machine learning simulators trained around mean squared error. Those missed behaviors matter for latency-sensitive systems, where average performance alone gives an incomplete picture of network stability.

Accurate Neural Architecture Search, or ANAS, automates the search for models that capture delay distributions. It combines a hybrid architecture search space with a similarity constraint intended to correct evaluation inaccuracies in weight-sharing search. A Wasserstein loss then trains the chosen model against the full delay distribution, giving distributional behavior a direct role in optimization.

The discovered architecture reduces overall validation loss by 25.8% relative to DeepQueueNet and lowers normalized Wasserstein distance by up to 69.8%. These results support improved modeling of both typical delays and tail behavior in the evaluated setting. The framework offers a way to design network-device simulators whose accuracy accounts for the performance spectrum relevant to protocol and algorithm validation.
icml-2026-optimizing-network-simulation-.tldr: ANAS searches for network simulation architectures that model full delay distributions, improving average and tail-sensitive prediction metrics.

paragraphs: Vision-language models commonly represent images as fixed grids of patch features. This paper examines whether that spatial format remains necessary after training. The authors observe that fine-tuned visual representations become more abstract and less spatially coherent, and that image-text aligned models can develop a few specialized tokens summarizing global image content.

RADIO1D builds on this observation by compressing an image into a variable-length, one-dimensional token sequence. It combines knowledge distillation from multiple teachers with an autoencoder design. The resulting representations support hierarchical summarization, allowing the number of tokens to change according to the desired balance between accuracy and computational cost.

The authors report accurate scene understanding even with a single token, improved composition-aware image retrieval, and competitive multimodal benchmark performance with reduced overhead and better accuracy. These findings support compact, adjustable representations as a useful alternative to fixed patch features in the evaluated tasks. The contribution connects an analysis of learned visual abstraction to a representation designed to exploit it.
icml-2026-radio1d-elastic-representation.tldr: RADIO1D compresses images into adjustable-length token sequences, supporting efficient vision-language processing and strong hierarchical scene summaries.

paragraphs: Efficient distillation compresses language models through structured pruning and lightweight tuning. The paper finds that strong general benchmark performance can coexist with severe losses in multi-step reasoning, which it calls reasoning collapse. It investigates this failure through the geometry of the compressed model’s hidden representations.

The analysis focuses on a leading method that reduces representation width using projection matrices. Random initialization can produce uneven singular values, reducing the effective rank of the resulting representations. In plain terms, the representation loses usable diversity, making tokens harder to distinguish. The authors provide a theoretical explanation connecting this initialization behavior to effective-rank collapse.

Reasoning-preserved Efficient Distillation, or RED, initializes the projections as channel-selection matrices using activation information. The theory supports this choice as a way to mitigate rank collapse. Experiments on Llama and Qwen models show substantial recovery of reasoning while preserving high training efficiency and state-of-the-art general ability. The findings make initialization a consequential part of compression, especially when reasoning quality matters beyond aggregate benchmark scores.
icml-2026-reasoning-preserved-efficient-.tldr: RED uses activation-aware projection initialization to mitigate representation collapse and recover reasoning in efficiently distilled language models.

paragraphs: Segmenting an object becomes difficult when it shares visual patterns with its surroundings, as happens with camouflage. CurriSeg addresses this setting by changing how the model learns. The paper emphasizes training dynamics as a source of robustness, complementing a research focus that has often centered on architectural changes.

The first phase selects training examples using statistics of their losses over time. This helps distinguish difficult but informative examples from noisy or ambiguous ones. The second phase deliberately suppresses high-frequency image components, encouraging the model to rely on broader structural and contextual information. This challenging fine-tuning stage follows the earlier phase of controlled capability development.

CurriSeg combines that second phase with Sharpness-Aware Minimization to encourage flatter optimization minima and better generalization. Experiments show consistent improvements across diverse context-entangled segmentation benchmarks without adding parameters or increasing total training time. The results support coordinating example selection and later perceptual challenges to improve robustness when local appearance offers weak evidence about object boundaries.
icml-2026-refining-context-entangled-con.tldr: CurriSeg improves difficult object segmentation through adaptive example selection followed by training that emphasizes broader structure and context.

paragraphs: Multimodal language models can generate statements that conflict with an image or with common sense. Preference-based training can reduce these hallucinations, but preparing response comparisons often requires human review or stronger external models. The paper also identifies problems when externally corrected responses produce off-policy preference data for Direct Preference Optimization.

RLSF-V constructs preference data through feedback from the reference policy itself. Its local fuzzy semantic evaluation derives a hallucination-sensitive confidence signal from internal logits, the scores used in generating text. This signal ranks diverse generated responses, producing preference pairs for fine-tuning without human labels or external model supervision for their construction.

Training on a dataset at the 10,000-example scale yields competitive results on generative and discriminative benchmarks relative to existing human-feedback and AI-feedback reinforcement learning baselines. The contribution is a self-contained way to obtain hallucination-oriented training preferences. The findings show that internal model signals can support useful response ranking in this setting while reducing dependence on more costly external evaluators.
icml-2026-rlsf-v-mitigating-hallucinatio.tldr: RLSF-V uses internal confidence signals to create its own response preferences for reducing multimodal hallucinations without external supervision.

paragraphs: Text-guided segmentation requires understanding which object a description refers to and locating its pixels. A single prediction leaves little opportunity to recover if the model initially selects the wrong region. RSAgent treats segmentation as an iterative process in which reasoning, tool use, and visual feedback inform one another.

The agent queries a visual toolbox, observes the results, and revises its hypothesis about the target’s location. Earlier observations remain available to guide later steps, supporting both relocalization and mask refinement. Training begins with supervised fine-tuning on synthesized multi-turn segmentation trajectories, followed by agentic reinforcement learning using fine-grained rewards tailored to the task.

The authors report zero-shot performance of 66.5% gIoU on the ReasonSeg test set, a stated 9% improvement over Seg-Zero-7B, and 81.5% cIoU on RefCOCOg. They report state-of-the-art results on both in-domain and out-of-domain benchmarks. These findings support giving a segmentation model opportunities to inspect and revise its decisions as part of the learned procedure.
icml-2026-rsagent-learning-to-reason-and.tldr: RSAgent improves text-guided segmentation by repeatedly using visual tools, observing feedback, and refining its target localization and masks.

paragraphs: A correctly reassembled object remains correct if the entire assembly is rotated or translated. Standard training losses can nevertheless penalize such globally transformed solutions. Fixing one fragment as an anchor can introduce bias and break symmetry under fragment reordering, motivating a framework that handles global pose directly in its geometry.

The authors combine two constructions. Global Gauge Fixing deterministically aligns configurations using an intrinsic generalized-inertia rule. A quotient-invariant flow-matching objective then projects dynamics onto directions that change the assembly’s shape while excluding overall rigid motion. This lets learning focus on relative fragment arrangement throughout the trajectory, factoring out global pose at each timestep.

The framework has efficient closed-form versions in two and three dimensions. Experiments show improved accuracy on polygonal jigsaw puzzles and three-dimensional fracture reassembly. The significance is that an equivalence already present in the task—assemblies differing only by global position and orientation—becomes part of the learning formulation itself, rather than something the model must handle through arbitrary anchoring.
icml-2026-se-n-invariant-flow-matching-a.tldr: This flow-matching framework factors out global rigid motion so object reassembly models learn relative shape changes without arbitrary fragment anchoring.

paragraphs: Shapley-based explanations assign importance to inputs and can measure interactions among them, but their computation involves exponentially many input subsets. TN-SHAP-G addresses this cost for graph-structured inputs by learning a compact approximation of how a predictor behaves when parts of its input are masked.

Given a predictor and a fixed masking scheme, the method fits a multilinear surrogate represented as a tensor network whose connections mirror the input graph. After training from a small number of predictor queries, it computes first-order importance and higher-order interaction indices deterministically through the surrogate’s multilinear extension. These computations require no further predictor queries and introduce no Monte Carlo sampling variance.

Experiments on molecular benchmarks show close agreement with exact Shapley values on small graphs and efficient scaling to larger graphs where sampling approaches become infeasible. The deterministic calculation applies to the learned surrogate, so its agreement with the original predictor remains tied to approximation quality. The results support using graph structure to make repeated attribution and interaction calculations more tractable.
icml-2026-tn-shap-g-graph-structured-ten.tldr: TN-SHAP-G learns graph-aligned tensor-network surrogates that enable efficient, deterministic Shapley attribution and interaction calculations.
